title: A Termite's Worst Molt-Day: New Chemical Blocks Exoskeleton Growth, Spares Humans
summary: Drywood termites are masters of hide-and-seek, silently devouring wooden structures from the inside out. But their secretive lifestyle hinges on a vulnerable biological process: molting. Researchers at the University of California, Riverside have exploited this weakness with bistrifluron, a chemical that blocks the formation of chitin—the key component of insect exoskeletons. In a study published in the Journal of Economic Entomology, the treatment wiped out about 95% of a colony without the mammalian toxicity concerns tied to traditional fumigants. The secret lies in the termite body plan. Unlike humans, who have internal skeletons, insects wear their support system on the outside. That exoskeleton is built from chitin, a tough polysaccharide also found in fungal cell walls and squid beaks. When termites grow, they must shed their old shell and build a new one—a process they undergo about seven times. Bistrifluron disrupts this by inhibiting chitin synthesis. 'Once the termites reach a certain stage, they have to molt. They cannot avoid that,' said Dong-Hwan Choe, UCR entomology professor. 'With a lethal dose, they'll try to shed their old exoskeleton but won't have a new one ready to protect them.' The effect isn't instant. Researchers observed that exposed termites first became sluggish and fed less. Over time, molting failed and the insects died. In no-choice tests, bistrifluron caused 99% mortality over 60 days; in choice tests with a 0.1% concentration, it achieved 96% mortality. Crucially, the chemical spreads socially. Termites engage in proctodeal trophallaxis—a mouth-to-anus feeding behavior that transfers food and gut microbes. When only 5% of a colony was exposed, the entire group reached 100% mortality by day 90. This means a spot treatment could potentially collapse a large, hidden colony without tenting an entire home. Traditional fumigation is costly, disruptive, and toxic. 'Low-impact strategies like this one will become an attractive option,' Choe said. Moreover, bistrifluron may remain active in wood, offering residual protection. While full colony collapse takes about two months—slower than some methods—the trade-off is a targeted, environmentally friendlier solution that could revolutionize termite control.
why_it_matters: A safer, targeted termite treatment could reduce our reliance on toxic fumigants, protecting families, pets, and the environment while still stopping destructive infestations. It also shows how studying insect biology can lead to pest control that spares mammals.

background_read: Drywood termites cause more than $5 billion in property damage worldwide annually, eating wood from the inside out while remaining hidden.

Universities like UC Riverside (a public research university in Southern California) study insects that threaten homes and agriculture; their findings often appear in journals like the Journal of Economic Entomology, a peer-reviewed publication focused on practical insect science.

Traditional whole‑house fumigation uses sulfuryl fluoride, a gas toxic to humans that requires tenting and evacuation. Chitin‑synthesis inhibitors, however, have been used safely for years — for example, lufenuron stops flea eggs from hatching in pet medications.

The termite behavior proctodeal trophallaxis is unique among social insects: food and gut microbes are shared mouth‑to‑anus, so a small dose of insecticide can pass from one individual to the whole colony, a feature already used in bait stations.

perspectives.description: With no mammalian toxicity, bistrifluron avoids the health risks of tent fumigation, and its ability to spread socially means a small spot treatment can collapse an entire hidden colony. Residual protection in the wood offers long-term defense.

The two-month delay to full colony collapse is slower than immediate fumigation. If the chemical does not reach every crevice through trophallaxis, some termites might survive, and the method's effectiveness in very large or deep colonies is still being established.

Insects wear their skeleton on the outside, making molting a universal weak point. Chitin inhibitors have been used in agriculture and flea control for decades; this study applies the same principle to a particularly well‑hidden home‑invader.

If bistrifluron proves durable inside wood, it could be incorporated into building materials or into preventive treatments during construction. Researchers hope that low‑impact chemicals like this will eventually replace the most toxic pesticides.
